title: The whole human condition
hookLine: every person carries the whole form of the human condition (Essays 3.2)

cards: Montaigne opens an essay in book three with a strange apology. Other writers, he says, try to shape a human being, to show what a person ought to be. He only describes one: himself, and not a very well made one.
If he could make that man over, he says, he'd make him quite different, but it's done now. So why read page after page about one ordinary man with his faults and his kidney stone?
His answer is a single sentence, and it's today's word.

teach.b: First, the passing. Montaigne says he doesn't paint being; he paints passing. Not a fixed portrait, but a man changing from day to day, even minute to minute.
If he contradicts himself, it's because he's describing a moving thing honestly. Second, the sentence.

teach.h: EACH PERSON CARRIES THE WHOLE FORM.
teach.b: Every person, he writes, carries the whole form of the human condition. Not a slice. The whole.

A farmer, a king, a man with a stone in his side: each holds the full shape of being human, its fears and appetites, its kindness and its death. So a plain, private life isn't too small to study. It's a complete specimen.
Third, two ways to hear it.
Some readers hear humility: nothing in me is foreign to anyone else. Others hear dignity: nobody is a rough version of a person, nobody is only a part. Montaigne seems to mean both.
He studies himself not because he's special but because he isn't. Fourth, the stranger. At the pharmacy counter, the person ahead of you is easy to see as a back, a delay, a type.
That stranger carries the whole of it too: a childhood, a worry about money, a joke they tell well, a body that will one day stop. You don't have to know their story.
Only that it's a whole one.

how: Readers of Montaigne often quote his line that each person carries the whole form of the human condition as the reason his self-portrait speaks to strangers.

games.q: what does “the whole human condition” mean?
o: the full list of illnesses a person can suffer
the fixed rank each person is born into for life
the idea that every person carries all of being human

s: Montaigne says he describes an ideal person for others to copy
he says others shape a person; he only describes one, and not a well made one.
he says he paints passing, not being
he describes a man changing from day to day.
he says only great people carry the whole human condition
every person carries the whole form of it, however ordinary.

games.q: you want to understand human beings. Montaigne has a method. which is it?
o: study one ordinary life closely: his own.
survey as many people as possible.
games.why: he studies himself, not because he's special but because every person carries the whole form of the human condition.

practice: Bring to mind someone you saw recently and didn't know: a driver, a cashier, a person on the next bench.
Hold their face a moment, then let the rest come in without inventing a story: they were a child once, they worry about someone, something makes them laugh. Let them be whole, and breathe with that.

wordCard.voice: The whole human condition. Montaigne's claim that every person, however ordinary, carries all of it. Today's word.

orig.s: la forme entière de l'humaine condition
orig.say: lah FORM ahn-TYAIR duh loo-MEN kohn-dee-SYOHN
orig.note: Montaigne's French: the whole form of the human condition, from Essays 3.2.

carryVoice: Your line: the whole of it. In the king, the farmer, the stranger at the counter, and in you. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Montaigne, Essays 3.2, Of repentance (others shape man, I describe one; I paint passing, not being; each man bears the whole form of the human condition)
